source.title: AdaSGD: Bridging the gap between SGD and Adam

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; no garbling or cutoff apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures optimizer-related training and test performance and argues that generalization differences between SGD and Adam depend on the setting and can be reduced with global learning-rate adaptation. Its results refine V4, but most experiments compare optimizers rather than directly measuring train–test gaps.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper’s own real-data optimizer comparisons and its CIFAR-10 optimizer-direction measurement. Statements and measurements cited from earlier work are not rows. The reported results do not test random-label memorization, width beyond interpolation, convolutional versus fully connected architecture, batch size, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removal of memorized examples.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares Adam and momentum SGD on held-out image-classification and language-model performance under restricted hyperparameter searches. This tests V4 without requiring an explicit train–test gap: equal or better training performance is an optional part of V4, not a prerequisite.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors argue that SGD has useful implicit regularization while Adam is more robust to learning-rate choice, and that globally adaptive AdaSGD can combine these benefits and achieve performance comparable to or better than transitional methods. This is not a claim that AdaSGD wins every comparison or is the optimal adaptation scheme.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares SGD, Adam, and a proposed global-learning-rate adaptation (AdaSGD) on synthetic optimization problems and real datasets; it does not reproduce the natural-versus-random-label experiments or other claim-version interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and learning-rate selection change relative optimizer performance. Adam performs best on WikiText-2 with tuned hyperparameters; SGD performs best on MIMIC-3 and CIFAR-10 with tuned hyperparameters. With fixed learning rates, AdaSGD is best on MIMIC-3 and WikiText-2, while SGD is best on CIFAR-10. AdaBound sensitivity to final learning rate and transition parameter is described in Figure 4, but its numeric figure-only values are not extracted.

fits_no_version.finding: On clinical prediction, tuned SGD, Adam, and AdaSGD achieve AUCs of 0.852, 0.847, and 0.849; fixed-rate results are 0.841, 0.847, and 0.849.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizer rankings on clinical time-series prediction depend on learning-rate selection, with overlapping reported confidence intervals.

fits_no_version.finding: The proposed globally adaptive AdaSGD often approaches the better-performing optimizer across image and language tasks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Global learning-rate adaptation can combine useful performance properties of SGD and Adam.

fits_no_version.finding: Update projection onto the ten largest-absolute-eigenvalue directions is 0.0502 for AdaSGD and 0.0006 for Adam.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adam updates depend more strongly on directions outside the leading Hessian eigenspace than AdaSGD updates.

record.problems: The real-data experiments report task-level held-out metrics, but not paired training metrics or explicit train–test gaps. Results use validation-selected models and only 3 random seeds for CIFAR-10 and WikiText-2, 5 for MIMIC-3; the reported confidence intervals are bootstrapped. The optimizer-direction measure is not itself a generalization-gap measure.
record.rows_left_out: No additional numeric results measuring V4’s optimizer-related held-out performance were omitted. Figure 4 gives AdaBound sensitivity values only graphically, so no exact values are recorded. Appendix D tables report more dataset and architecture comparisons, but the text states they are consistent with findings already represented here; the main claims and conditions are covered by Table 2. Synthetic quadratic-loss optimization losses are not natural-data generalization results.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and the corresponding natural-label and random-label held-out controls.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.

Whether Adam's worse held-out performance accompanies equal or better training performance; broader tuning of Adam's other hyperparameters; decoupled weight decay. Switching methods are tested in Table 2 but omitted from the rows.
Batch-size comparisons and recipe adaptations under controlled epoch budgets.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence, and augmentation interactions.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, its correlation with generalization gaps, and comparisons with norm and margin measures.
Removal of highly memorized examples versus random removals.

missing.what: Table 2's Swats and AdaBound results are omitted despite directly addressing V4's switching-recovery clause. On CIFAR-10, Swats reaches 93.29% and AdaBound 94.82%, versus SGD 94.20% and Adam 93.43%. On WikiText-2, their perplexities are 122.77 and 267.43, versus SGD 123.52 and Adam 108.37. Record these separately by method and dataset.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for V4. Its results support both the image-classification disadvantage and the explicit word-level language-model exception; mixing these into a single limits_scope verdict obscures the claim's wording. Appendix D results were explicitly declared omitted in rows_left_out, so they are not listed as newly missing. Rows use optimizer names as subjects; these should be identified as optimizers applied to the stated architectures. The supplied text does not provide paired numerical training metrics for Table 2.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweep beyond the zero-training-error threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture and local connectivity.

No language-model comparison showing Adam outperforming SGD; no comparison of broad tuning strategies beyond the reported learning-rate and L2 grid search; no weight-decay-decoupling or Adam-to-SGD switching intervention.
Large-batch versus small-batch comparisons under fixed epoch budgets.
Dropout additions/removals and interactions with data augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness or comparison with norm- and margin-based generalization measures.
Removing high-influence memorized examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.
